# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Saudi Arabia
Education shifted from traditional Islamic Kuttabs to a formal system combining secular and religious curricula, with girls’ schools since 1964. Overseen by the Ministry of Education and Technical and Vocational Training Corporation, expenditure reached 5.1% of GDP in 2006. Literacy attained 85% by 2007, amid persistent gender and regional disparities. Reforms like Tatweer emphasize English, ICT, practical skills, and inclusivity but face criticism for rote learning and religious focus. Since 2021, primary education is mandatory and multilingual; secondary offers general and technical tracks with religious content. Higher education hosts 24 public universities with growing female enrollment, though female labor participation remains low. Support includes programs for gifted and special needs students; private international schools mainly serve expatriates.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Bangladesh
The system includes general and Islamic streams under different ministries alongside international curricula and madrasahs blending secular and religious studies. NGOs and UNICEF back non-formal education for vulnerable children and refugees. Primary passing requires 33%, with spending from 0.94% to 2.2% of GDP. Literacy rose from 51.77% (2011) to 74.66% (2022). Challenges include teacher absenteeism, poverty, scarce resources, limited tertiary seats, rural dropouts, and gender parity gaps.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## New Zealand
Māori education predated secular compulsory schooling legislated in 1878. Early childhood education follows the Te Whāriki curriculum; secondary culminates in NCEA with Cambridge and IB options. About 85% attend free state schools; zoning affects choice and property values. Māori immersion education improves outcomes relative to mainstream schooling. Tertiary education aligns with the NZ Qualifications Framework, supported by subsidies, interest-free loans, and allowances. Achievement gaps and bullying persist despite high teaching quality.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Canada
Education is provincially legislated with constitutional protections for disability and minority language education. Religious separate and secular charter schools exist regionally. Levels span early childhood to Grade 12 with programs including IB and AP. Universities grant degrees up to doctorates; vocational colleges blend instruction with apprenticeships. Equity programs address identity issues amid concerns of transparency and grade inflation. Private schooling (6% at Grade 10) is mainly in Quebec with higher outcomes.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Mexico
Education evolved from prehispanic and colonial church-led systems to a secular socialist model with free textbooks. Preschool begins at age 3; primary and secondary offer general, vocational, and distance options. Intercultural Universities support Indigenous access despite low enrollment. Inclusive policies integrate special needs students despite coordination gaps. Primary attendance exceeds 90%; secondary about 62%, limited by rural infrastructure. Literacy reached 95% by 2018 with gender parity. The SNTE union often resists reforms. English-medium international schools and prestigious private universities have expanded.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Czech Republic
Elementary schooling covers nine grades with broad curricula feeding into diverse secondary tracks (vocational, professional, lyceum, grammar) culminating in Maturita exams for university. Special education increasingly integrates disabled students. Public universities are tuition-free for Czech speakers under 26; private institutions charge fees. Doctoral degrees require discipline-specific exams. The academic year runs September to June.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Japan
Formal education dates to the 6th century; Western-style compulsory education began post-Meiji Restoration. Post-WWII reforms democratized and decentralized education, later re-centralized with moral education emphasis. The academic year starts in April: six years primary, three lower secondary, three upper secondary; universities offer degrees through doctorates. Compulsory subjects include Japanese, math, science, English (since 2011), and moral education. Entrance exams are critical, supported by cram schools, aiding performance but linked to mental health issues. Over 2.89 million enroll university nationwide. Special Needs Education fosters inclusion. English-medium international schools mainly operate outside compulsory frameworks.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Poland
Compulsory education covers 12 years, ending at 18 after abolishing gimnazjum. Upper secondary tracks include general (liceum), technical (technikum), vocational, and special schools, culminating in Matura exams for university access. Higher education aligns with the Bologna process, featuring bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees graded from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (highest). English and German are widely taught. Reforms in 1999 and 2017 revamped curricula and structure, addressing school violence.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Netherlands
Education is coordinated by the Ministry of Education with municipal involvement. Public, religious (special), and general-special schools receive equal funding and are free; private schooling is minimal. Compulsory education starts at 5 (often 4) until 16 (partial) or 18 (full). Elementary schooling covers foundational skills and English; Cito or alternatives determine secondary placement into VMBO (vocational), HAVO (general), or VWO (pre-university). Adult education (VAVO) offers completion paths. Postsecondary includes MBO vocational training, HBO professional colleges, and WO research universities with accredited degrees. Streaming occurs around age 12, influenced by test results and socioeconomic status, raising equity and misplacement concerns. National performance declined over two decades.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Pakistan
Education spans primary (ages 3–10, 67.5% completion), secondary, and technical/vocational tracks culminating in national or British exams. Bachelor programs vary from 2-year Pass to 4-year Honours. Teacher education is theory-heavy and underqualified; vocational education faces outdated content. Non-formal education includes community and corporate initiatives; madrasas serve many low-income students but emphasize rote learning and have extremist links. Female literacy and workforce participation remain low despite higher medical enrollment. Transgender rights improved legally but social marginalization persists. Distance learning enhances access, especially for women in remote areas, amid challenges like slowed research and teacher pay cuts.
Spending is about 2% of GDP, below targets, causing infrastructure deficits. Science education reflects religious influences, rejecting evolution while affirming Islam-science compatibility. Textbooks display biases including anti-Semitic portrayals, Holocaust omission, glorification of Hitler for German pride, conflict framing, minority marginalization, and gender stereotypes. Literacy rose from 17.9% (1951) to 60.65% (2023), higher among males and urban populations. Provincial disparities persist; Punjab and Islamabad outperform others. Youth literacy reached ≥85% in multiple districts. Mean years of schooling improved nationally, highest in Islamabad and Punjab, lowest in less developed regions. Despite progress, Pakistan trails peers like Malaysia and Indonesia due to poverty, feudalism, patriarchy, teacher absenteeism, poor infrastructure, and governance weaknesses. Pakistani international schools number 439 (2015), mostly English-medium; many pursue higher education in China via recognized online platforms.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## South Korea
Education reflects Confucian meritocracy and social mobility, starting with traditional village schools. Japanese occupation centralized education, limiting Korean access. Post-liberation reforms democratized and decentralized education, then recentralized it, balancing academic and vocational tracks responsive to industrial demands. By the mid-1980s, literacy exceeded 90%, with secondary and tertiary enrollment at developed-nation levels. Government spending reached 4.5% of GNP, supporting economic modernization through human capital investment.
Intense "education fever" in the 1980s–90s accompanied democratization and growth, leading to reforms abolishing on-campus ROTC, legalizing teacher unions, removing anti-communist texts, and decentralizing curricula. South Korean students excel internationally, but pressures contribute to high suicide rates and family financial burdens. A shift to competency-based education is underway.
Education starts with infant and nursery schooling (ages 3–5), followed by elementary (grades 1–6), middle (grades 7–9), and high school (grades 10–12). Compulsory subjects include Korean, math, moral education, science, physical education, music, arts, and English from grade 3. Corporal punishment was banned in 2011 and mobile phones prohibited in class from 2023.
Secondary completion is 98%, with competitive general and special-purpose high schools often charging high tuition. Vocational high schools (~20%) provide academic and practical training for workforce entry or further study.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## South Korea
### Vocational Education: Meister Schools
Meister Schools, modeled on Germany’s apprenticeship system, aim to reduce youth unemployment, offering near-guaranteed employment and university access. Despite 100% post-graduation employment, stigma limits enrollment (~5%). Graduates often secure major-company jobs and may earn more than university graduates.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## South Korea
### Higher Education
South Korea’s largely U.S.-influenced higher education system comprises mainly private universities awarding bachelor’s, master’s, doctoral, and professional qualifications. Admission depends on College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT) and academic/extracurricular records, with prestigious "SKY" universities dominating. Vocational and industrial universities offer alternatives amid societal stigma.
Community and junior colleges provide 2–3-year vocational programs in varied fields, with moderately competitive admissions reserving places for vocational high school graduates. There are 154 mostly private junior colleges (600,000+ students) and 227 undergraduate institutions serving 2.25 million students; over 327,000 enroll in graduate programs.

### English Education

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## South Korea
### Social and Systemic Challenges
The system is intensely competitive; over 95% of middle and high school students attend hagwons, imposing heavy financial burdens and stress linked to declining birthrates. Special Purpose High Schools face criticism for elitism and high costs. A severe mismatch exists between student majors and employment, ranking among OECD’s lowest.
Student well-being suffers from excessive academic pressure, limited physical education, and weak student rights, reflected in low happiness scores, teacher dissatisfaction, bullying, and creativity suppression. Health policies, such as banning coffee in schools, aim to improve conditions.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Russia
Education includes preschool, primary, basic, and secondary stages starting at age 6 or 7 with compulsory schooling for at least nine years (commonly eleven). Urban preschool shortages persist despite increased enrollment. Secondary education covers nearly 59,260 general schools with state-controlled curricula and a 5-point grading scale. Specialized secondary tracks include academics and arts. After nine years, students may continue general schooling or vocational colleges with three-year combined work-study programs. Male vocational students face conscription with possible university deferment.
The Unified State Examination (USE), implemented nationally since 2008, standardizes university admissions, enhancing fairness but facing transparency criticisms. Special education integrates disabled students, though those with severe intellectual disabilities often remain excluded. Tertiary enrollment exceeds 50%, double the OECD average, across 1,000+ institutions. The 2000s saw rapid growth of state institutions, followed by consolidation into federal universities from 2006 to enhance quality, with Moscow State University among the leading federal universities.
Historically, Russia offered a single five- or six-year specialist diploma equivalent to Western MSc/MA. Since 2003, Bologna Process reforms introduced four-year bachelor’s and two-year master’s degrees; however, bachelor’s degrees are often undervalued, with limited academic mobility and rising master’s costs.
Postgraduate education awards two scientific degrees: Candidate of Sciences (Ph.D. equivalent) and Doctor of Sciences (habilitation equivalent), requiring original research and publications. Academic titles (docent, professor) depend on scholarly achievement. Military postgraduate education is separate.
The 2021 Science Outreach Law regulates knowledge dissemination, raising concerns about censorship and restrictions targeting alleged anti-Russian propaganda.
Following the 2022 Ukraine invasion, patriotic education intensified via “Important Conversations” lessons promoting national identity and traditional values, criticized as militaristic, with some students facing police scrutiny or expulsion for non-attendance.

# Education in Saudi Arabia, Bangladesh, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico, the Czech Republic, Japan, Poland, the Netherlands, Pakistan, South Korea, and Russia: Comparative Overview
## Russia
### Linguistic Diversity
Russia supports education in over 6,300 schools offering instruction in various minority languages serving approximately 24.8 million speakers, and over 10,500 schools teach these languages as subjects. Major languages include Tatar, Bashkir, Chuvash, Avar, and Yakut. Smaller languages have limited instructional schools but receive some subject teaching, reflecting efforts to preserve diverse linguistic and ethnic heritage.
